item.title: Hamas on the Streets of Paris
item.description: On 20 October 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about a wide range of issues, including the causes of the ongoing civil unrest in France, Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s comments in Athens about restoring the greatness of Western civilization, and, of course, the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 20 October 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about a wide range of issues, including the causes of the ongoing civil unrest in France, Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s comments in Athens about restoring the greatness of Western civilization, and, of course, the wars in Iran and Ukraine. My favorite part of the interview came when the Judge played a clip of Prime Minister Netanyahu—that same man who convinced President Trump to attack Iran on 28 February—making the ludicrous claim that Hamas is running loose in the streets of Paris.

item.title: Trump Just Can’t Win
item.description: On 18 October 2026, I appeared on “Switzerland” with host Tom Switzer to discuss the war in Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 18 October 2026, I appeared on “Switzerland” with host Tom Switzer to discuss the war in Ukraine. We examined in detail President Trump’s efforts to facilitate the flow of Russian diesel fuel and oil into global markets, as well as the problems this strategy is creating for him with Ukraine, European elites, and much of the American national security establishment. Given that the Iran war and the Houthi-Saudi war are both heading due south, Trump appears to be in trouble everywhere he turns on the foreign policy front. Worse still, he has no attractive way to resolve these problems, which only seem to grow more serious with time.

item.title: The West's Self-Inflicted Wounds
item.description: On 16 October 2026, I appeared on Glenn Diesen’s popular podcast to discuss the ongoing war in Ukraine, the various conflicts in the Middle East, and what they mean for Europe and the West more generally.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 16 October 2026, I appeared on Glenn Diesen’s popular podcast to discuss the ongoing war in Ukraine, the various conflicts in the Middle East, and what they mean for Europe and the West more generally. I argued that European elites and much of the US national security establishment are mistaken in believing that continuing to support Ukraine in its war against Russia serves the West’s interests. Not only is Ukraine likely to end up devastated, but that war—along with the conflicts in the Middle East involving Iran and the Houthis—is likely to inflict further damage on an international economy already under tremendous stress. Moreover, relations between Europe and Russia will remain poisonous for years, if not decades, to come, while NATO has been seriously weakened by the Ukraine war.

item.title: Talking Iran with Iran
item.description: On 11 October 2026, I appeared on Be Waqte Iran, Iran’s most-watched television program devoted to war and strategic affairs.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 11 October 2026, I appeared on Be Waqte Iran, Iran’s most-watched television program devoted to war and strategic affairs. The show airs live every evening on IRINN, Iran’s state-run, 24-hour television news channel. The host, Syed Sarbaz Rezvi, asked thoughtful and probing questions about the Iran war, which, unsurprisingly, were quite similar to those I regularly encounter in interviews with Western hosts. The interview is not available on YouTube, but it can be easily accessed through the X post linked here.

item.title: No End to Trump’s Troubles
item.description: On 13 October 2026, I was on Judging Freedom, talking with the Judge about recent developments in the wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Gaza genocide, and the Saudi-Houthi war.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 13 October 2026, I was on Judging Freedom, talking with the Judge about recent developments in the wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Gaza genocide, and the Saudi-Houthi war. The central question was whether there is any reason to believe President Trump is moving toward resolving these four conflicts in ways that serve American interests. My answer regarding all four of these disasters was a resounding no.

item.title: Trump vs. Zelensky—Again!
item.description: On 11 October 2026, I was on Switzerland with Aaron Maté and host Tom Switzer, discussing the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On 11 October 2026, I was on Switzerland with Aaron Maté and host Tom Switzer, discussing the wars in Iran and Ukraine. We focused especially on President Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing it to be sold on global markets. Although Trump’s move has enraged President Zelensky, almost every major European leader, and a number of prominent members of Congress, none of us think it would have a meaningful effect on the course of the war, which I believe Ukraine is destined to lose.

We also discussed how the recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which have been especially damaging, combined with Iran’s intensified attacks on shipping in the Persian Gulf region, have put the United States increasingly on the back foot.

Finally, we considered the Pentagon’s reported plan to livestream the execution of former U.S. Army Major Nidal Hasan, who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. We all agreed that such a spectacle would be outrageous and would further damage America’s moral standing in the world, which is already in tatters.

item.title: The West’s Fall from Grace
item.description: On 9 October 2026, I was on Ian Proud’s podcast, The Peacemonger. We discussed a variety of subjects, but our principal focus was on the dramatic decline in the West’s standing around the world in recent years. We explored the root causes of that decline and its likely consequences. Given the extraordinary sense of moral superiority that prevailed in the West after the Cold War ended, it is truly astonishing how far the West has fallen.

item.title: NATO Won’t Quit & Won’t Win
item.description: On 8 October 2026, I was on Lena Petrova’s popular podcast, World Affairs in Context, discussing the war in Ukraine and its implications not just for Ukraine’s future, but for NATO’s as well.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On 8 October 2026, I was on Lena Petrova’s popular podcast, World Affairs in Context, discussing the war in Ukraine and its implications not just for Ukraine’s future, but for NATO’s as well. I emphasized that NATO is deeply involved in the war, but that NATO and Ukraine working together cannot defeat Russia. As I have long argued, Russia is going to win an ugly victory, while Ukraine will end up a dysfunctional rump state.

Recent developments on the battlefield, in Europe, within the Trump administration, and inside Ukraine itself reinforce my argument that Ukraine’s position is steadily deteriorating while Russia’s is growing stronger. Importantly, this conversation took place before President Trump reached an agreement with President Putin to allow Russian diesel to flow into world markets, which is terrible news for Ukraine.

item.title: Don’t Mess with the Houthis
item.description: On October 6, 2026, I was on Rachel Blevins’ popular podcast discussing the war between the United States and Iran and the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On October 6, 2026, I was on Rachel Blevins’ popular podcast discussing the war between the United States and Iran and the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia. We devoted considerable attention to the Saudi decision to escalate its war against the Houthis. I find that decision puzzling. After all, the Saudis spent seven years (2015–2022) trying unsuccessfully to defeat the Houthis, who are arguably in a stronger position to fight Saudi Arabia today than they were during the earlier war.

We also discussed the danger that Iran—and possibly even the United States—could become directly involved in the Saudi-Houthi war, effectively merging the two ongoing conflicts into a much larger regional war. Meanwhile, the threats to the international economy continue to mount.

item.title: Yemen & Horizontal Escalation
item.description: On 6 October 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to end the Iran war on terms favorable to the US — which are doomed to failure — as well as the president’s increasing tendency to make outrageous comments, like his claim that it would be a small price to pay if Los Angeles and San Diego were destroyed in a war with Iran.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On 6 October 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to end the Iran war on terms favorable to the US — which are doomed to failure — as well as the president’s increasing tendency to make outrageous comments, like his claim that it would be a small price to pay if Los Angeles and San Diego were destroyed in a war with Iran.

More importantly, however, we talked about how the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia threatens to escalate across the region, possibly dragging both Iran and the US into the fight. Up to now, the war between Iran and the US and the war between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have not been closely linked. But the Houthi-Saudi war is seriously heating up and there is a real danger that Iran might be forced to come to the aid of the Houthis, which might then lead the US to enter the fight on the Saudi side. Or the Saudis might find themselves in serious trouble — even if Iran stays out of the fight — which could compel the US to come to Riyadh’s rescue, which might then cause Iran to come into the fray. It should be noted that Pakistan and Turkey, which are part of the “Makkah Alliance for Defense,” which they signed with Saudi Arabia on 7 August 2026, have already come into the fight, although on a limited basis so far. The potential for trouble here cannot be underestimated.

item.title: Trump’s Big Bluff on Iran
item.description: The Trump administration and its supporters – including the Wall Street Journal editorial page – are working overtime these days to spin the news around the Iran war to make it appear that the US is winning and Tehran had better submit to Washington’s demands before it is wrecked, maybe even “annihilated.” Indeed, Trump is preparing the option of bringing the military hammer down on Iran after the midterm elections if Tehran has not surrendered by then.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration and its supporters – including the Wall Street Journal editorial page – are working overtime these days to spin the news around the Iran war to make it appear that the US is winning and Tehran had better submit to Washington’s demands before it is wrecked, maybe even “annihilated.” Indeed, Trump is preparing the option of bringing the military hammer down on Iran after the midterm elections if Tehran has not surrendered by then.

In effect, Trump and his supporters are waging a “maximum pressure campaign” against Iran in the mainstream media.

This campaign is sure to fail. If anything, it reflects the Trump administration’s desperation. The president started a war the United States was bound to lose, and there is little he can do now to change that basic fact.

Trump’s propaganda campaign has two dimensions – one economic and the other military.

First, the administration argues that Iran is being economically strangled by the US naval blockade coupled with Operation Economic Outcast, the strategy announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on 24 August 2026. At the same time, it maintains that oil is once again flowing out of the Gulf at rates not far below those that prevailed on 27 February 2026. The implications are obvious: the economic punishment being inflicted on Iran will force it to capitulate soon, while the US economy – and the international community more generally – is well on its way to recovery.

Second, the US is now building up its military forces for a massive military strike after the mid-term elections, when Trump will be free of electoral constraints. This growing threat of a devastating US attack, coupled with the economic pain being inflicted on Iran, is designed to get Tehran to quit now, before its situation becomes even worse.

There are huge problems with this strategy. It sounds persuasive when the mainstream media dutifully purveys it, but it falls apart when one looks closely at what is actually happening.

Consider the military dimension. The headlines say the US is sending 10,000 additional troops and a third aircraft carrier – the USS Theodore Roosevelt – to the Persian Gulf region, creating the impression that Iran will soon be confronting three American carriers. Moreover, the additional troops – on top of the roughly 50,000 US troops already in the region – are portrayed as evidence that Trump is seriously considering putting boots on the ground.

The aircraft carrier story, however, is quite different from what the headlines suggest. The Roosevelt is reportedly being sent to replace the USS George Washington, while the supposed third carrier, the USS George H.W. Bush, has already left the Middle East and is now in Thailand. Thus, there is presently only one carrier in the region. Indeed, this is the first time during the war that the US has only one carrier in the Middle East, and it is difficult to imagine that there will be more than two – if even that many – after the midterm elections.

The larger problem is that the Iran war is severely straining the US Navy. Its senior leaders warn that the current operational tempo is not sustainable indefinitely. Carriers and other warships are being rotated through extremely long deployments, which cause significant maintenance and readiness problems that will have to be addressed at some point. This problem is compounded by the fact that US ships have lost access to nearby logistics facilities and increasingly depend on a supply chain that reaches back to Diego Garcia, which is about 2,500 miles from the Persian Gulf.

But even if three carriers are available to strike Iran, what could they accomplish in a renewed air campaign that the US and Israel could not accomplish together during the failed 40-day bombing campaign between 28 February and 8 April 2026? Some might argue that the US could finally destroy Iran’s oil infrastructure. The problem, however, is that Iran retains a second-strike capability and could retaliate by wreaking havoc on the oil infrastructure of the GCC states. One shudders to think what the consequences would be for the international economy.

On top of all this, the US faces a serious shortage of high-end weaponry, which is one of the main reasons it ended the 40-day bombing campaign and has shied away in recent weeks from engaging in tit-for-tat bombing exchanges with Iran. One would think that the shortage of critical munitions – both for striking Iran and defending against Iranian retaliation – would limit the scope and intensity of any renewed strategic bombing campaign, thereby reducing its chances of success.

Regarding ground forces, simply counting the number of U.S. military personnel in the Middle East is misleading when assessing the possibility of putting boots on the ground. What matters most in a ground war is the number of troops in actual ground-combat formations. I estimate that, of the roughly 50,000 U.S. military personnel already stationed in the region, about 5,000 belong to such formations: roughly 2,200 Marines and sailors in the 11th MEU, 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne, and possibly another 800 Army personnel in Kuwait associated with Task Force Spartan. Of the roughly 10,000 additional personnel now being sent to the region, another 2,200 belong to the 13th MEU. Most of the remainder are sailors assigned to the Theodore Roosevelt carrier and its supporting warships. Thus, given present deployment plans, I estimate that by late November the United States will have just under 7,500 personnel in ground-combat formations in the Gulf region—roughly 4,400 in the two MEUs and 2,800 Army personnel.

There is no way a ground force that small provides a promising option against a country with Iran’s population and geography. Even tripling that number to roughly 23,000—which is highly unlikely—would not fundamentally alter the problem. Retired Army General Barry McCaffrey estimates that securing the Strait of Hormuz would require roughly 150,000 troops and three to six months of fighting. For comparison, Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 with roughly 190,000 military personnel, and that force proved insufficient to hold much of the territory Russia initially captured. Iran has more than twice the population Ukraine had at the beginning of the Russian invasion, and its geography is considerably more forbidding for an invading army.

Simply put, the United States has not assembled anything remotely resembling the ground force required for a large-scale invasion of Iran. Indeed, from Tehran’s perspective, an American decision to launch such an offensive with anything resembling the forces presently available would present Iran with an opportunity to fight the United States under exceptionally favorable circumstances.

At the risk of beating a dead horse, two further points are in order. First, given how unpopular the Iran war is with the American public, there would almost certainly be a huge uproar if large numbers of US soldiers began coming home in body bags. Second, how are the Marines, who are aboard amphibious assault ships, supposed to land on Iranian territory if the missile and drone threat from Iran is forcing the US Navy to keep those large and vulnerable ships far from the Iranian coast?

Let’s turn to the economic dimension. There is no question that the US is doing great damage to Iran’s economy and inflicting enormous hardship on the Iranian people. But that has been true for a long time. The key question is whether that punishment can coerce Iran into surrendering to American demands.

There is no evidence that Iran is caving in to American pressure, and there are three reasons to doubt that it will. First, it is exceedingly difficult to find a case in the historical record in which an economic blockade by itself caused the target state to surrender. Second, Iran sees the US and Israel as existential threats to Iran – hardly surprising given the genocidal language Trump has used when talking about Iran – and states that believe their survival is at stake are exceptionally difficult to coerce. Third, Iran has a formidable escalation option if the economic pain becomes too great: it can attack the oil and gas infrastructure of the Gulf states and Israel, as well as their highly vulnerable desalination plants.

In short, it is difficult to see economic pressure alone forcing Iran to accept Trump’s terms. That is probably one reason the United States is once again talking about using military force. But, as I argued above, that option holds little promise of producing a favorable outcome.

Finally, there is no question that more oil is flowing out of the Gulf today than was the case in early September. But both Iran and the Houthis are working hard to reverse that trend. Iran is attacking US-escorted tankers on a daily basis, while the Houthis are targeting vital oil infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia. Moreover, despite the increased flow of oil out of the Gulf, gasoline prices remain very high, and a host of other economic problems show no signs of easing anytime soon, including high diesel prices, persistent inflation, elevated mortgage rates, and dangerously high bond yields across much of the West.

All of this is to say that the Trump administration has powerful economic incentives to shut this war down as soon as possible. Indeed, it would hardly be surprising if there were a growing sense of desperation behind closed doors among Trump and his advisers.

This, of course, helps explain why the Trump administration and its allies are waging a media campaign designed to persuade Iran that its days are numbered and that it had better concede to American demands before it is too late. The facts, however, tell a different story. The success of this strategy therefore depends on Trump being able to bamboozle the Iranians into believing that Godzilla is closing in on them. There is little reason to think Tehran will be hoodwinked.

item.title: The West Has Lost Its Way
item.description: On September 30, 2026, I was on Glenn Diesen’s popular podcast, talking with him about America’s emerging position in the world, given that it cannot help Ukraine defeat Russia and has been unable to defeat Iran in the Middle East.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On September 30, 2026, I was on Glenn Diesen’s popular podcast, talking with him about America’s emerging position in the world, given that it cannot help Ukraine defeat Russia and has been unable to defeat Iran in the Middle East. My argument is that the United States is in deep trouble and that its strategic position is likely to deteriorate further. It has been a long time since first-rate strategic thinking guided U.S. foreign policy.

The situation is not much better for the Europeans. They have had the good sense to stay out of the Iran war, but in my view they have behaved remarkably foolishly toward Ukraine and Russia.

item.title: Trump Talks Genocide -- Again!
item.description: On 29 September 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about Iran.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded:
On 29 September 2026, I was on “Judging Freedom” talking with the Judge about Iran. We focused considerable attention on President Trump’s genocidal threat against Iran that he made at the UN on 22 September 2026. I noted that according to my count this was the seventh time he indicated he was going to wipe Iran off the face of the Earth. Remember that he said on 7 April 2026 that, a “whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again." It is also of paramount importance to never forget that Trump is complicit in the Israeli genocide in Gaza. Thankfully, he has backed off on all his threats to eliminate Iran from the planet.

In fact, I do not believe that the US has the capability to destroy Iran with conventional weapons, but that raises the question of whether he would use nuclear weapons to achieve that end. As I told the Judge, I cannot imagine the US doing that, although I am sure there are a good number of people who think I am naive and that Trump is not above carpet bombing Iran with nuclear weapons.

We also talked about the recent revelations that Prime Minister Netanyahu ignored warnings by high level officials from both Egypt and the UAE before 7 October 2023 that Hamas was getting ready to attack Israel. I noted that this is one reason Netanyahu has resisted setting up an independent commission to determine why Israel was caught with its pants down on 7 October. If such a commission is ever established, it will surely show that Netanyahu bears great responsibility for the disaster his country suffered on that fateful day.

item.title: Bombing to Lose
item.description: On 27 September 2026, I was on “Switzerland” with the host, Tom Switzer, and the distinguished author and columnist, Patrick Cockburn.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 27 September 2026, I was on “Switzerland” with the host, Tom Switzer, and the distinguished author and columnist, Patrick Cockburn. We talked mainly about Iran, focusing special attention on President Trump’s promise to employ massive military force against Iran after the mid-term elections and win the war once and for all. Since we have no ground option, this can only mean restarting the strategic bombing campaign that Trump began (with Israel) on 28 February 2026 and ended on 8 April 2026. Of course, that initial bombing campaign failed as will the next one, if the president is foolish enough to start it. The sad truth is that the president can’t face the fact that the Israelis — mainly Prime Minister Netanyahu — bamboozled him into starting a war the US cannot win and therefore it makes sense to cut a deal with Iran sooner rather than later.

item.title: Gloom & Doom in Iran
item.description: On 24 September 2026, I was on “The Chris Hedges Report,” where I talked to Chris at length about why the Trump administration has no winning strategy in Iran.
item.dc:creator: John J. Mearsheimer
item.content:encoded: On 24 September 2026, I was on “The Chris Hedges Report,” where I talked to Chris at length about why the Trump administration has no winning strategy in Iran. It certainly has no military option, which is why it is limiting itself to putting great pressure on Iran’s economy with a blockade coupled with Secretary of the Treasury Bessent’s strategy of cutting the Iranian economy off from the rest of the world. But that strategy won’t work either. And all the while, the US is pushing the international economy closer and closer to the brink.
